title: Find Anagram Mappings
statement: The arrays `nums1` and `nums2` hold the same values with the same multiplicities, only in a different order (values may repeat). Return an array `mapping` of the same length where `mapping[i]` is an index `j` with `nums2[j] === nums1[i]`. When a value repeats, several mappings are possible and any valid one is accepted.
constraints: nums2 is a rearrangement of nums1
notes:
## Intuition

For each value of `nums1` we need some position of the same value in `nums2`. Searching `nums2` from scratch for every value costs O(n²). Instead, index `nums2` once: a hash map from each value to the list of positions where it appears answers every lookup in O(1).

## Approach

1. Walk `nums2` and append each index `j` to `positions.get(nums2[j])`, creating the list the first time a value appears.
2. Walk `nums1`. For each `value`, take one index from its list with `pop()` and push it to `mapping`.
3. Return `mapping`. Because each index is removed once used, equal values even get different positions, so the result is a true one-to-one matching (one valid answer among possibly many).

## Example 1, step by step

`nums2 = [50, 12, 32, 46, 28]` gives `positions` = {50: [0], 12: [1], 32: [2], 46: [3], 28: [4]}. Walking `nums1 = [12, 28, 46, 32, 50]` pops 1, 4, 3, 2 and 0, so `mapping = [1, 4, 3, 2, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass to build the map and one pass to read it.
- Space: O(n) for the map of positions.

## Pitfalls

- Values can repeat. A map from value to a single index still gives a valid answer, but storing a list keeps the matching one-to-one.
- `mapping[i]` is an index into `nums2`, not a value.
- Do not sort either array: the indices must refer to the original order of `nums2`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `positions` | map from a value to the indices of `nums2` that still hold it |
| `j` | index into `nums2` while building the map |
| `value` | the current element of `nums1` |
| `mapping` | the answer being built, one index per element of `nums1` |

narration.2: Prepare a map from each value to the indices where it sits in nums2.
narration.3: Visit every index of nums2 once.
narration.4: First time we see this value: give it an empty list.
narration.7: Record that this value can be found at index j.
narration.10: The answer starts empty and will get one index per element of nums1.
narration.11: Take the values of nums1 in order.
narration.12: Take an unused index of the same value from nums2 and record it.
narration.14: Every element of nums1 now points to a matching position in nums2.
